source.title: What One Cannot, Two Can: Two-Layer Transformers Provably Represent Induction Heads on Any-Order Markov Chains
source.authors: C. Ekbote; Marco Bondaschi; Nived Rajaraman; Jason D. Lee; Michael Gastpar; A. Makkuva; Paul Pu Liang

record.tranche_reason: Provides a theoretical construction and a simplified training analysis of induction-like behavior on synthetic Markov data; it does not reproduce the original studies’ model-training and loss-by-token measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports theoretical representation and convergence results, attention-map observations, layer-count comparisons, and results under data noise. It cites phase-transition and induction-head findings from other work; those cited findings are not recorded as results here. It does not measure abrupt formation, a training-loss bump, loss by token position, large-transformer ICL, or few-shot task learning.
record.test_reason: The study tests, by theory and by training small two-layer transformers on synthetic Markov data, whether two-layer models form a previous-context first layer plus a second-layer matching head that implements the induction rule (V1). It also tests how data noise changes the learned induction pattern and the loss (V5). It does not measure formation timing, large models, or few-shot tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a two-layer, single-head transformer (using MLP non-linearities) can represent any-order conditional k-gram, that is, a k-th-order induction head. They also conclude that gradient descent on a reduced variant learns a first-order induction head. Experiments show one-layer models fail to form the pattern, and alignment and loss degrade as data departs from Markov structure.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical conditional k-gram constructions, a reduced two-stage gradient analysis, and synthetic Markov-sequence experiments, rather than the original training-loss and induction-head measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise level and type change the reported loss gap and attention alignment: token substitution worsens the loss gap as its probability increases; transition perturbations show little loss-gap change at α = 0.1 but larger gaps and substantial alignment deterioration at α = 0.25 and 0.5.

fits_no_version.finding: Quantizing to 8 bits keeps the second-layer attention map's Frobenius distance to the ideal map near full precision (3.86 vs 3.77). At 2–4 bits the distance is about 4.6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction-head attention structure is preserved under moderate weight and activation quantization.

record.code_released: not stated (the text says code is available at a link but gives no URL)
record.problems: The main training result is for a reduced model with components fixed at approximately optimal values, not the full transformer. Empirical results concern synthetic binary Markov sources and the text does not state model size for the attention-map experiments. Several attention-map findings are qualitative; the study gives no phase-transition or loss-by-token measurements.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix H.1 includes additional attention-map plots for first-, second-, and third-order sources, but separate plot-only outcomes are not included; the main text gives an explicit qualitative description for the third-order example (R3-R4). Appendix H.4 reports quantization results on Frobenius distance to an attention map, which do not directly measure a version tested here.

untested.parts: Attention-only models are not tested: all constructions and experiments use MLPs, ReLU and layer norm. The [A][B]…[A]→[B] rule is tested only on binary Markov sources, not on repeated-token text.
Not tested: no formation timing, abruptness, synchronized ICL gain or loss bump.
Not tested: no large models and no share of ICL attributed to induction heads.
Not tested: one GPT-2-style setup only.
Formation timing under different data or setups is not tested. Natural-data properties are not tested. Persistence of ICL over training is not tested.
Not tested. The first-order gradient analysis has two stages, but they are imposed by the training algorithm, so it is not evidence on V7.

missing.what: Under token substitution, second-layer attention alignment with the ideal map is stated to degrade as the substitution probability rises. No row records alignment at substitution probabilities above 0.
The text says the model is more robust to transition noise than to token substitution, a comparison between the two noise types.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The noise experiments compare the model's loss with the true-transition loss, and the text does not say whether noise is applied only in training or also in evaluation. Because of this, the rise in the loss gap may partly reflect the noise itself rather than worse learning. The attention-alignment evidence is qualitative, from figures. The first-order two-stage dynamics come from a schedule set by hand, so they are not evidence on V2 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: The construction is not attention-only: it uses MLPs, ReLU and layer normalization. It does not establish that the circuit forms by composing with an earlier previous-token head in the specific sense stated; its training analysis is for a simplified first-order model.
No formation-time sweep, narrow-window or abruptness measure, loss-by-token measure, synchronized ICL gain, or training-loss bump.
No large transformers or measurement of what proportion of their in-context learning is carried by induction heads.
Experiments use a GPT-2-based synthetic-data setup; no comparison across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.

Tests noise in synthetic second-order Markov data and gives theoretical results under specified Markov assumptions. It does not test whether ICL persists across real-world data or compare formation times across training setups.
No few-shot task-learning evaluation or comparison with other mechanisms for task learning.
No test of whether induction-head formation comprises multiple or overlapping transitions.

rows.subject: two-layer, single-head transformer (Theorem 3 construction)
rows.operation_detail: Constructs a two-layer, single-head transformer representing the conditional k-gram model for any k ≥ 1.

conditions.value: relative positional encodings, MLP blocks and layer normalization

rows.measure: Representation of conditional k-gram / k-th-order induction-head behavior
rows.value: Theorem 3 states the conditional k-gram model can be represented; the proof obtains the estimator in the limit of increasing softmax temperature.
rows.note: Supports representation of the induction-like conditional k-gram function in this architecture. The construction uses MLPs and nonlinearities, so it does not test the attention-only setting specified in V1.

source_check.correct: Theorem 3 constructs a two-layer, single-head transformer with MLPs, relative positional encodings and layer normalization; embedding dimension 6S + 3. V1 state: cannot_determine, because its attention-only setting is untested.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Theorem 3 and proof sketch; Appendix B
source_check.problem: An MLP-based construction does not establish an incomplete effect in V1's attention-only architecture.

rows.subject: reduced two-layer transformer (first-order Markov gradient analysis)
rows.operation_detail: Trains positional scalars, then freezes them and trains the second-layer attention scalar in a simplified model with other components treated as approximately optimal.
rows.measure: Convergence to the conditional 1-gram / induction-head behavior and excess loss
rows.value: Theorem 4 gives L(θ̂) − L* ≲ log(T + 1)/(T + 1)^(cγ); the text also states that the model approximates the conditional 1-gram with vanishing error as sequence length grows.
rows.note: The result is for the reduced, reparameterized model, with several components fixed at approximately optimal values; it is not a training-dynamics result for the full transformer.
rows.check: This bears on the composition order in V1. In the reduced first-order model, stage 1 provably learns previous-token attention and stage 2 then sharpens the induction head (App. C.2–C.3). However, this is a reduced model with fixed components and a two-stage schedule set by hand.

source_check.correct: The reduced model achieves the stated excess-loss bound. Previous-token attention is learned during the first training stage; positional parameters are then frozen while the second-layer scalar is trained. V1 state: cannot_determine.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, training algorithm and Theorem 4; Appendix C introduction and C.2–C.3
source_check.problem: The model retains fixed MLP components, and sequential formation follows an imposed training schedule rather than testing V1 in an attention-only model.

rows.note: The attention map is consistent with the proposed construction’s first-layer context aggregation, but is not itself a measure of the second-layer induction matching behavior.

relationships.condition: Two-layer single-head transformers with MLPs, trained on random Markov sources (orders 1–3)
relationships.reason: The first layer aggregates preceding tokens and the second layer resembles the ideal induction pattern (R3, R4). One layer does worse and lacks that pattern (R5, R6). In the reduced first-order model, previous-token attention forms first and then the induction head (R2).
relationships.display_finding: The first layer aggregated preceding tokens and the second resembled ideal induction, while one-layer models performed worse and lacked that pattern; under sequential training in the reduced first-order model, previous-token attention formed before the induction head.

source_check.condition: Two-layer single-head transformers with MLPs, trained on random Markov sources (orders 1–3)
source_check.reason: R2–R6 concern MLP-based models, whereas V1 explicitly specifies attention-only transformers. They support an architectural extension, but do not test that literal version; R2 also imposes sequential training.

relationships.condition: Higher-order (k>1) induction with one head per layer
relationships.reason: In the construction, the MLP's ReLU and layer norm are needed to rebuild the matching representation. The authors call these non-linearities critical, so composition of attention heads alone is not the whole mechanism here (R1).
relationships.display_finding: For orders above one, the construction used MLP ReLU and layer normalization to rebuild the matching representation, without establishing that all possible constructions require them.
